content: Turkey coronaviruses belong to the Coronaviridae family and primarily infect turkeys, particularly young poults, causing gastrointestinal disease. These viruses are also referred to as Turkey Enteritis Virus, Bluecomb Disease Virus, or Turkey Coronaviral Enteritis. Transmission occurs horizontally through fecal matter and can spread either directly or indirectly via contaminated objects (fomites). The disease has been reported in regions such as North America, Europe, and Brazil. A closely related condition in birds is avian infectious bronchitis. The clinical signs of gastrointestinal disease caused by turkey coronavirus include diarrhea, loss of appetite (anorexia), and lethargy. Affected birds within a flock often exhibit darkened skin and ruffled feathers, and the majority of the group is typically impacted. In the United States, turkey coronavirus is recognized as one of the causative agents of Poult Enteritis and Mortality Syndrome (PEMS), which affects birds up to one month of age. Mortality rates can be significant in poults. Birds that recover from the infection develop lifelong immunity but may act as carriers of the virus. Diagnosis of turkey coronavirus infection can be achieved through various methods, including necropsy, histological examination, indirect immunofluorescence, immunoperoxidase staining, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), and polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Treatment is primarily supportive and may include the use of heat lamps, antibiotics, and milk replacers to manage symptoms and secondary infections. Since the virus can persist within a flock, it is recommended that farms undergo depopulation following an outbreak to prevent further spread.
